The Physics Was There All Along

By the Twice Baked AI Team

Post 2 ended on a specific observation, easy to miss the significance of at the time: every method tried so far, classical or learned, GAN or VAE or diffusion, had one thing in common. All of it operated on processed, display-domain images, the kind of image a radiologist actually looks at on a monitor. None of it ever touched the actual signal a detector produces.

That turns out to matter enormously, and getting specific about why is where this post starts.

What a “processed image” actually is, and what it hides

A modern X-ray detector doesn’t hand a radiologist a raw measurement. Between the detector and the screen sits a vendor’s image-processing pipeline: tone mapping, contrast enhancement, sometimes content-adaptive adjustments that behave differently depending on what anatomy is in view. This processing is genuinely useful, it’s why images are readable at all, but it also does something easy to overlook: it partially obscures the true, physical relationship between signal and noise described back in Post 1.

Every method in Posts 1 and 2 worked on the right side of this diagram. This post is about working on the left side instead.

Once an image has been through that pipeline, you’re no longer looking at “signal plus noise” in any simple sense, you’re looking at “signal plus noise, then reshaped by a rendering process that has its own, separate effect on both.” Building a physically accurate noise model on top of an already-processed image means modeling two things tangled together instead of one thing cleanly. The alternative, and the subject of this whole post, is to go earlier: work directly on the raw, 16-bit signal a detector produces, before any of that rendering happens, and already carrying every bit of native detector resolution.

What “raw” and “16-bit” actually mean, in numbers

It’s worth being concrete about this rather than leaving “raw” as a vague, better-sounding word. The processed images every method in Posts 1 and 2 worked with are typically 8-bit: each pixel’s brightness is stored as one of 256 possible values. The raw signal this project works with instead is 16-bit: each pixel is stored as one of 65,536 possible values, 256 times more brightness resolution.

The actual numbers behind “raw” and “processed.” This is a 256-times difference in how finely brightness can be represented, not a small technical footnote.

Why does this matter for noise modeling specifically? Because the noise law described below depends on measuring small differences in signal precisely. If an image has already been compressed down to 256 brightness levels, subtle real variations get rounded together into the same value, a visible symptom of this called banding or posterization, and the physically accurate relationship between signal and noise becomes harder to recover cleanly:

An illustrative demonstration of the underlying concept (the top bar uses an exaggerated 16-level version to make the banding visible at this size; real 8-bit images band more subtly, but the same principle applies). Raw 16-bit data avoids this entirely.

Real detector signal values are commonly referred to in ADU, short for “analog-to-digital unit”, simply the raw numeric brightness value a sensor’s electronics assign to a given amount of detected signal, before any further processing. Every number in the noise law below is expressed in these raw ADU units, not in the familiar 0-255 range a processed image uses.

The noise law, explained slowly

Post 1 introduced two physical noise sources: quantum noise (from counting photons) and electronic read noise (from the detector’s own circuitry). This section makes that precise enough to actually build a training dataset from.

Statisticians describe quantities that vary randomly around some typical value using variance, essentially a measure of how much spread or “wobble” a quantity has. A larger variance means a wider range of possible values around the average; a smaller variance means values cluster tightly. The standard deviation is just the square root of the variance, and it’s the more intuitive number: it tells you the typical size of the noise, in the same units as the signal itself.

The relationship this project locked in, after calibration against real detector measurements, is a straight line:

variance = 0.147 × signal + 30

Walking through the formula with real numbers, rather than leaving it abstract.

Read that formula as two separate physical effects, added together:

  • 0.147 × signal: the quantum-noise term from Post 1. As the signal (proportional to how many photons landed on that part of the detector) goes up, the noise variance goes up too, proportionally. This is the photon-counting statistics described in Post 1, now given an exact slope.
  • + 30: the electronic read-noise floor. Even at a signal of zero, there’s always at least this much variance, from the detector’s own circuitry, independent of how many photons showed up.

The read-noise floor made visible: even at a signal of essentially zero, real noise is still present, exactly as the “+30” term in the formula predicts.

This exact mathematical shape, noise variance rising as a straight-line function of signal, is not something invented for this project. It’s a well-established model in the broader raw-image denoising research literature, going back to foundational work on modeling sensor noise as a combination of a Poisson (photon-counting) component and a Gaussian (electronic) component, which simplifies to exactly this kind of straight-line relationship between signal and variance.1 Multiple independent papers on raw-sensor denoising, across ordinary photography and medical imaging alike, arrive at the same functional form.2 This project’s contribution wasn’t inventing a new kind of physics, it was carefully calibrating the two constants, 0.147 and 30, against this project’s own real detector.

Why the noise has texture, not just strength

A second, separate refinement matters just as much as getting the amount of noise right: getting its texture right. Simple noise models treat every pixel’s noise as completely independent of its neighbors. Real detector noise isn’t quite like that: a detector’s physical construction (the layer that converts X-rays into visible light before a sensor reads it) causes a small amount of blur even in the noise itself, neighboring pixels’ noise values are weakly related, not fully independent.

This project models that relationship with a fixed, seven-value “kernel”, a small set of weights describing how much a pixel’s noise should be blended with its immediate neighbors before being applied to the image.

The kernel weights, visualized directly. About 61% of each pixel’s noise comes from its own random draw; the rest is a weighted blend from its six nearest neighbors.

In plain terms: to generate this project’s noise, you don’t just draw a random number for each pixel independently. You draw a whole grid of random numbers, then blend each pixel’s value slightly with its close neighbors using these seven weights, weighted most heavily toward the center. The result looks subtly different from plain “static,” and that subtle difference is exactly the texture gap Post 1’s earliest attempts couldn’t close.

The concept of spatial correlation, made visible. This animation uses a stronger blending effect than the project’s actual 7-tap kernel, whose real effect is subtle at normal viewing scale, to make the underlying idea clear: correlated noise has soft, blob-like structure; independent noise doesn’t.

The physical chain of cause and effect behind the 7-tap kernel: a real detector component (the scintillator) is the actual reason correlation exists at all.

This isn’t a made-up correction, either. Published research on X-ray detector physics specifically identifies the physical cause: many detectors convert X-rays to visible light using a scintillator layer before that light is measured, and light generated at one point inevitably spreads a little before reaching the sensor underneath it, a physical effect with its own established name, the detector’s point spread function. That same body of research explicitly identifies a Poisson-Gaussian noise mixture, the same two-source model from the previous section, as the standard, most suitable model for exactly this kind of detector.3 This project’s 7-tap kernel is a compact, practical stand-in for that same physical spreading effect.

Putting it together: the full recipe

The complete recipe, in order. Every step traces back to something explained above.

The same five stages, applied to real data, in motion.

One detail in that last step is easy to miss but matters a great deal: after adding noise, the image is scaled back up to its original brightness level. Without this step, a model could learn an unwanted shortcut, “make the image brighter” instead of “remove the noise”, since lower dose naturally means a dimmer raw signal before any noise is even considered. Removing that shortcut was a deliberate, necessary design choice, not an incidental detail.

Training doesn’t happen at just one noise level. This project uses an 8-level dose curriculum, spaced logarithmically (evenly spaced in log-space, not linear space) rather than evenly. In concrete terms: each level is roughly the same percentage smaller than the one before it, around 72% of the previous level’s dose each time, rather than the same absolute amount smaller. This packs more distinct steps into the low-dose end, where a small change in dose fraction produces a much bigger change in noise behavior than the same-sized change would at full dose.

Log-spacing puts more resolution where the noise behavior changes fastest: the low-dose end.

Seeing the actual formula at work

Everything above is abstract until you see it applied to real training data. Here is an actual training patch, at all 8 dose levels, straight from this project’s own training pipeline, not a reconstruction or an approximation:

The raw signal itself, at all 8 dose levels. Notice how subtle the visible difference is, this is a real, deliberate teaching moment, explained below.

That subtlety is itself an important, honest observation, not a visualization failure. Raw sensor data hasn’t been through the display-rendering pipeline described earlier in this post, the same pipeline that stretches and remaps brightness for a human to look at comfortably. Viewed in its native form, a raw image can look deceptively similar across a wide range of real signal differences, precisely because nothing has adjusted the display range to reveal them.

Once the same eight patches are put through a realistic display-rendering step, the actual degradation becomes unmistakable:

The same real data, same eight levels, rendered the way a viewer would actually see it. The noise growth described by the formula above is now directly visible.

The same real data, in motion.

This is a genuinely useful lesson about raw data generally, not just about this project: the physically correct signal and the visually informative signal are not automatically the same thing. Getting the physics right, as this post has been about, is necessary. Rendering that physics into something a human can actually evaluate by eye is a separate, additional step, and conflating the two risks either underselling a real effect (raw form) or overselling a rendering choice as if it were the underlying physics (vendor form).

Honest results: very good, not perfect

The team validated this recipe by injecting a known amount of noise and then measuring how closely the actual result matched the intended target, expressed as a ratio (measured divided by intended, so 1.0 would be a perfect match):

Reported honestly rather than smoothed over: precision is very good across most of the curriculum, and dips slightly below target at the single hardest, lowest-dose level.

This is worth sitting with for a moment, because it would have been easy to simply not mention it. At the lowest dose level, the low end of the measured range (0.84) falls just under a 0.90 target threshold the team set for itself. This isn’t a sign the whole approach is unreliable, every other measurement across every other dose level lands comfortably inside the target range, it’s a specific, narrow, honestly-reported edge case at the single most extreme setting, exactly the kind of finding this series exists to report plainly rather than quietly round away.

One thing we genuinely don’t know

In the interest of the same honesty: the original detector-characterization work that produced the two locked constants, 0.147 and 30, and the specific shape of the 7-tap kernel, is not something we can point to directly in this project’s own surviving records. The numbers themselves are consistent everywhere they appear, calibrated once and then relied upon repeatedly across every part of the pipeline described in this post, but the original characterization study that produced them isn’t something we can hand you a citation for. We’d rather say that plainly than imply a cleaner paper trail than actually exists.

Why this became the current, sole approach

Every method in Posts 1 and 2 worked around the edges of a problem this approach addresses directly: getting the noise physically right, on the actual signal a detector produces, rather than approximating it on an already-processed image or hoping a learned model would discover the right texture on its own from too little data. This is currently the only synthetic-degradation approach in active, ongoing use across the whole project, every other method described so far has been superseded, abandoned, or left half-finished.

That doesn’t mean the story ends here. Getting the noise physics right didn’t automatically solve everything. A new, more subtle problem emerged once this foundation was solid, one about how aggressively a model should trust its own correction, and it’s where three completely different approaches, tried independently, converged on the exact same wall. That convergence is where Post 4 picks up.

This is Post 3 of an ongoing series documenting the dataset-creation history behind our low-dose X-ray restoration research. Next: “Full Circle,” on self-supervised methods, domain adaptation, and where this history stands today.
